# OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes Integration for Elastic

## Overview

The OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes integration enables collection of cluster state, node pool configuration, node lifecycle, and Kubernetes audit log data from [OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes Service (MKS)](https://www.ovhcloud.com/en-gb/public-cloud/kubernetes/) via the OVHcloud REST API.

This integration is designed for organizations running workloads on OVHcloud — Europe's largest cloud provider — and seeking full observability and audit trail coverage without deploying in-cluster agents.

### Compatibility

This integration is compatible with the OVHcloud API v1.0 (EU, CA, and US regions). It requires an OVHcloud service account with OAuth2 `client_credentials` support, available in all OVHcloud regions.

### How it works

The integration uses the CEL input to poll the OVHcloud Management REST API using OAuth2 client credentials authentication. It iterates over all clusters in a given Public Cloud project and collects state snapshots for clusters, node pools, and nodes. The audit stream uses a presigned URL generated by the OVHcloud API to download recent Kubernetes audit events.

## What data does this integration collect?

The OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes integration collects the following data:

* **Cluster** — lifecycle status, Kubernetes version, region, upgrade readiness, and network configuration
* **Node pool** — autoscaling counters (desired/current/available nodes), capacity status, and billing mode
* **Node** — per-node lifecycle status, Kubernetes version, and pool membership
* **Audit** — Kubernetes API server audit events including user identity, resource accessed, verb, and response code

### Supported use cases

- Cluster health monitoring and upgrade readiness alerting
- Autoscaling anomaly detection (underscaled / overscaled pools)
- Node lifecycle tracking (provisioning, errors, upgrades)
- Kubernetes audit trail for security analysis and compliance (GDPR, SOC 2)
- User access auditing: who accessed which Kubernetes resource and when

## What do I need to use this integration?

- An OVHcloud account with a Public Cloud project containing at least one Managed Kubernetes cluster
- An OVHcloud IAM service account with `client_id` and `client_secret` (OAuth2 client credentials)
- The service account must have read access to the Public Cloud project's Kubernetes resources
- Elastic Agent installed on a host with outbound HTTPS access to the OVHcloud API

## How do I deploy this integration?

### Agent-based deployment

Elastic Agent must be installed. For more details, check the Elastic Agent [installation instructions](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/fleet/current/elastic-agent-installation.html). You can install only one Elastic Agent per host.

### Set up steps in OVHcloud

1. Log in to the [OVHcloud Control Panel](https://www.ovh.com/manager/).
2. Navigate to **IAM** → **Service Accounts** → **Create service account**.
3. Note the `client_id` and `client_secret` generated.
4. Assign the service account read permissions on the Public Cloud project's Kubernetes resources.
5. Note your Public Cloud project ID (`serviceName`) from the project dashboard.

#### Vendor resources

- [OVHcloud API Getting Started](https://help.ovhcloud.com/csm/en-gb-api-getting-started-ovhcloud-api)
- [OVHcloud Service Account (OAuth2) Setup](https://help.ovhcloud.com/csm/en-manage-service-account)
- [OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes Documentation](https://help.ovhcloud.com/csm/en-public-cloud-containers-orchestration)
- [Kubernetes Audit Log Forwarding](https://help.ovhcloud.com/csm/en-public-cloud-kubernetes-forwarding-audit-logs)

### Set up steps in Kibana

1. In Kibana, go to **Integrations** and search for **OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes**.
2. Click **Add OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes**.
3. Configure the following required settings:
   - **OVHcloud API URL**: Regional API base URL (EU default: `https://eu.api.ovh.com/1.0`)
   - **OVHcloud Project ID**: Your Public Cloud project `serviceName`
   - **OAuth2 Client ID**: Service account `client_id`
   - **OAuth2 Client Secret**: Service account `client_secret`
   - **OAuth2 Token URL**: Regional token endpoint (EU default: `https://www.ovh.com/auth/oauth2/token`)
4. Enable the data streams you want to collect (cluster, nodepool, node, audit).
5. For the **audit** data stream, also provide the **Cluster ID** (`kubeId`) of the target cluster.
6. Save and deploy the policy.

### Validation

After deploying the integration, verify data is flowing:

1. In Kibana **Discover**, filter on `data_stream.dataset: ovh_managed_kubernetes.cluster` to see cluster state events.
2. Check `data_stream.dataset: ovh_managed_kubernetes.audit` for Kubernetes audit events.
3. If no data appears within one polling interval (default 5 minutes), check the Elastic Agent logs.

## Troubleshooting

- No data is being collected: Verify the `service_name` (project ID) is correct and the service account has read permissions on the project's Kubernetes resources.
- Authentication failures (401): Check that `client_id`, `client_secret`, and `token_url` match your OVHcloud region (EU/CA/US).
- Audit stream returns empty: The `kube_id` must be a valid cluster UUID from the target project. Verify it using the OVHcloud API Console or the cluster data stream. Also ensure audit logs are enabled on the cluster (OVH Manager → Kubernetes → cluster → Logs tab) and that the cluster is on the Standard plan or higher.
- Rate limiting (429 responses): Increase the polling interval to 10m or higher for large projects with many clusters.

## Performance and scaling

For more information on architectures that can be used for scaling this integration, check the [Ingest Architectures](https://www.elastic.co/docs/manage-data/ingest/ingest-reference-architectures) documentation.

## Setup

For more details about the CEL input settings, check the [Filebeat documentation](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/beats/filebeat/current/filebeat-input-cel.html).

Before configuring the CEL input, make sure you have:
- Network connectivity to the target API endpoint
- Valid authentication credentials (API keys, tokens, or certificates as required)
- Appropriate permissions to read from the target data source

### Collecting logs from CEL

To configure the CEL input, you must specify the `request.url` value pointing to the API endpoint. The interval parameter controls how frequently requests are made and is the primary way to balance data freshness with API rate limits and costs. Authentication is often configured through the `request.headers` section using the appropriate method for the service.

NOTE: To access the API service, make sure you have the necessary API credentials and that the Filebeat instance can reach the endpoint URL. Some services may require IP whitelisting or VPN access.

To collect logs via API endpoint, configure the following parameters:

- API Endpoint URL
- API credentials (tokens, keys, or username/password)
- Request interval (how often to fetch data)
</details>


### API usage

These APIs are used with this integration:

* `GET /cloud/project/{serviceName}/kube` — List all cluster IDs
* `GET /cloud/project/{serviceName}/kube/{kubeId}` — Get cluster details
* `GET /cloud/project/{serviceName}/kube/{kubeId}/nodepool` — List node pools
* `GET /cloud/project/{serviceName}/kube/{kubeId}/node` — List nodes
* `POST /cloud/project/{serviceName}/kube/{kubeId}/log/url` — Generate a temporary URL to download audit logs (kind: `audit`). Requires a Standard plan cluster with audit logs enabled. The returned URL (`get.logs.ovh.com`) is only accessible from within the OVH network.

### Vendor documentation links

- [OVHcloud API Console (EU)](https://eu.api.ovh.com/console-preview/?section=%2Fcloud&branch=v1)
- [OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes Product Page](https://www.ovhcloud.com/en-gb/public-cloud/kubernetes/)
- [OVHcloud IAM Documentation](https://help.ovhcloud.com/csm/en-manage-service-account)

### Data streams

#### cluster

The `cluster` data stream provides a state snapshot of each OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes cluster in the configured Public Cloud project. Events include cluster status, Kubernetes version, region, upgrade readiness, and network configuration.

##### cluster fields

**Exported fields**

| Field | Description | Type |
|---|---|---|
| @timestamp | Date/time when the event originated. This is the date/time extracted from the event, typically representing when the event was generated by the source. If the event source has no original timestamp, this value is typically populated by the first time the event was received by the pipeline. Required field for all events. | date |
| cloud.provider | Name of the cloud provider. Example values are aws, azure, gcp, or digitalocean. | keyword |
| cloud.region | Region in which this host, resource, or service is located. | keyword |
| cloud.service.name | The cloud service name is intended to distinguish services running on different platforms within a provider, eg AWS EC2 vs Lambda, GCP GCE vs App Engine, Azure VM vs App Server. Examples: app engine, app service, cloud run, fargate, lambda. | keyword |
| data_stream.dataset | The field can contain anything that makes sense to signify the source of the data. Examples include `nginx.access`, `prometheus`, `endpoint` etc. For data streams that otherwise fit, but that do not have dataset set we use the value "generic" for the dataset value. `event.dataset` should have the same value as `data_stream.dataset`. Beyond the Elasticsearch data stream naming criteria noted above, the `dataset` value has additional restrictions:   \* Must not contain `-`   \* No longer than 100 characters | constant_keyword |
| data_stream.namespace | A user defined namespace. Namespaces are useful to allow grouping of data. Many users already organize their indices this way, and the data stream naming scheme now provides this best practice as a default. Many users will populate this field with `default`. If no value is used, it falls back to `default`. Beyond the Elasticsearch index naming criteria noted above, `namespace` value has the additional restrictions:   \* Must not contain `-`   \* No longer than 100 characters | constant_keyword |
| data_stream.type | An overarching type for the data stream. Currently allowed values are "logs" and "metrics". We expect to also add "traces" and "synthetics" in the near future. | constant_keyword |
| event.category | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the second level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.category` represents the "big buckets" of ECS categories. For example, filtering on `event.category:process` yields all events relating to process activity. This field is closely related to `event.type`, which is used as a subcategory. This field is an array. This will allow proper categorization of some events that fall in multiple categories. | keyword |
| event.dataset | Name of the dataset. If an event source publishes more than one type of log or events (e.g. access log, error log), the dataset is used to specify which one the event comes from. It's recommended but not required to start the dataset name with the module name, followed by a dot, then the dataset name. | constant_keyword |
| event.kind | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the highest level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.kind` gives high-level information about what type of information the event contains, without being specific to the contents of the event. For example, values of this field distinguish alert events from metric events. The value of this field can be used to inform how these kinds of events should be handled. They may warrant different retention, different access control, it may also help understand whether the data is coming in at a regular interval or not. | keyword |
| event.module | Name of the module this data is coming from. If your monitoring agent supports the concept of modules or plugins to process events of a given source (e.g. Apache logs), `event.module` should contain the name of this module. | constant_keyword |
| event.type | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the third level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.type` represents a categorization "sub-bucket" that, when used along with the `event.category` field values, enables filtering events down to a level appropriate for single visualization. This field is an array. This will allow proper categorization of some events that fall in multiple event types. | keyword |
| input.type | Type of filebeat input. | keyword |
| orchestrator.cluster.id | Unique ID of the cluster. | keyword |
| orchestrator.cluster.name | Name of the cluster. | keyword |
| orchestrator.cluster.version | The version of the cluster. | keyword |
| orchestrator.type | Orchestrator cluster type (e.g. kubernetes, nomad or cloudfoundry). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.audit_logs_subscribed | Whether audit log streaming is enabled for the cluster. | boolean |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.control_plane_is_up_to_date | Whether the control plane is running the latest version. | boolean |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.created_at | Timestamp when the cluster was created. | date |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.customization.api_server.admission_plugins.disabled | List of disabled Kubernetes admission plugins. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.customization.api_server.admission_plugins.enabled | List of enabled Kubernetes admission plugins. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.ip_allocation_policy.pods_ipv4_cidr | IPv4 CIDR block allocated for pod networking. | ip_range |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.ip_allocation_policy.services_ipv4_cidr | IPv4 CIDR block allocated for service networking. | ip_range |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.is_up_to_date | Whether the cluster nodes are running the latest version. | boolean |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.kube_proxy_mode | kube-proxy networking mode (e.g. iptables, ipvs). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.next_upgrade_versions | Available Kubernetes versions the cluster can be upgraded to. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.nodes_subnet_id | Subnet ID used for cluster nodes (null when private network is not configured). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.nodes_url | Node endpoint hostname for the cluster. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.plan | Cluster billing plan (e.g. free, hour, month). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.status | Cluster lifecycle status (e.g. READY, INSTALLING, UPDATING). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.update_policy | Cluster upgrade strategy (e.g. ALWAYS_UPDATE, MINIMAL_DOWNTIME). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.cluster.url | API server endpoint hostname for the cluster. | keyword |

#### node

The `node` data stream provides per-node lifecycle status, Kubernetes version, and pool membership for all nodes across all clusters.

##### node fields

**Exported fields**

| Field | Description | Type |
|---|---|---|
| @timestamp | Date/time when the event originated. This is the date/time extracted from the event, typically representing when the event was generated by the source. If the event source has no original timestamp, this value is typically populated by the first time the event was received by the pipeline. Required field for all events. | date |
| cloud.instance.id | Instance ID of the host machine. | keyword |
| cloud.machine.type | Machine type of the host machine. | keyword |
| cloud.provider | Name of the cloud provider. Example values are aws, azure, gcp, or digitalocean. | keyword |
| cloud.service.name | The cloud service name is intended to distinguish services running on different platforms within a provider, eg AWS EC2 vs Lambda, GCP GCE vs App Engine, Azure VM vs App Server. Examples: app engine, app service, cloud run, fargate, lambda. | keyword |
| data_stream.dataset | The field can contain anything that makes sense to signify the source of the data. Examples include `nginx.access`, `prometheus`, `endpoint` etc. For data streams that otherwise fit, but that do not have dataset set we use the value "generic" for the dataset value. `event.dataset` should have the same value as `data_stream.dataset`. Beyond the Elasticsearch data stream naming criteria noted above, the `dataset` value has additional restrictions:   \* Must not contain `-`   \* No longer than 100 characters | constant_keyword |
| data_stream.namespace | A user defined namespace. Namespaces are useful to allow grouping of data. Many users already organize their indices this way, and the data stream naming scheme now provides this best practice as a default. Many users will populate this field with `default`. If no value is used, it falls back to `default`. Beyond the Elasticsearch index naming criteria noted above, `namespace` value has the additional restrictions:   \* Must not contain `-`   \* No longer than 100 characters | constant_keyword |
| data_stream.type | An overarching type for the data stream. Currently allowed values are "logs" and "metrics". We expect to also add "traces" and "synthetics" in the near future. | constant_keyword |
| event.category | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the second level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.category` represents the "big buckets" of ECS categories. For example, filtering on `event.category:process` yields all events relating to process activity. This field is closely related to `event.type`, which is used as a subcategory. This field is an array. This will allow proper categorization of some events that fall in multiple categories. | keyword |
| event.dataset | Name of the dataset. If an event source publishes more than one type of log or events (e.g. access log, error log), the dataset is used to specify which one the event comes from. It's recommended but not required to start the dataset name with the module name, followed by a dot, then the dataset name. | constant_keyword |
| event.kind | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the highest level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.kind` gives high-level information about what type of information the event contains, without being specific to the contents of the event. For example, values of this field distinguish alert events from metric events. The value of this field can be used to inform how these kinds of events should be handled. They may warrant different retention, different access control, it may also help understand whether the data is coming in at a regular interval or not. | keyword |
| event.module | Name of the module this data is coming from. If your monitoring agent supports the concept of modules or plugins to process events of a given source (e.g. Apache logs), `event.module` should contain the name of this module. | constant_keyword |
| event.type | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the third level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.type` represents a categorization "sub-bucket" that, when used along with the `event.category` field values, enables filtering events down to a level appropriate for single visualization. This field is an array. This will allow proper categorization of some events that fall in multiple event types. | keyword |
| host.name | Name of the host. It can contain what hostname returns on Unix systems, the fully qualified domain name (FQDN), or a name specified by the user. The recommended value is the lowercase FQDN of the host. | keyword |
| input.type | Type of filebeat input. | keyword |
| orchestrator.cluster.id | Unique ID of the cluster. | keyword |
| orchestrator.type | Orchestrator cluster type (e.g. kubernetes, nomad or cloudfoundry). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.created_at | Timestamp when the node was created. | date |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.deployed_at | Timestamp when the node was successfully deployed. | date |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.id | Node UUID. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.is_up_to_date | Whether the node is running the latest Kubernetes version. | boolean |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.node_pool_id | Parent node pool UUID. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.project_id | OVHcloud Public Cloud project ID. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.status | Node status (e.g. READY, INSTALLING, ERROR). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.node.version | Kubernetes version running on the node. | keyword |

#### audit

The `audit` data stream provides Kubernetes API server audit events from a specific cluster, including user identity, resource accessed, HTTP verb, and response code. Events are downloaded via a presigned URL generated by the OVHcloud API.

##### audit fields

**Exported fields**

| Field | Description | Type |
|---|---|---|
| @timestamp | Date/time when the event originated. This is the date/time extracted from the event, typically representing when the event was generated by the source. If the event source has no original timestamp, this value is typically populated by the first time the event was received by the pipeline. Required field for all events. | date |
| cloud.provider | Name of the cloud provider. Example values are aws, azure, gcp, or digitalocean. | keyword |
| cloud.service.name | The cloud service name is intended to distinguish services running on different platforms within a provider, eg AWS EC2 vs Lambda, GCP GCE vs App Engine, Azure VM vs App Server. Examples: app engine, app service, cloud run, fargate, lambda. | keyword |
| data_stream.dataset | The field can contain anything that makes sense to signify the source of the data. Examples include `nginx.access`, `prometheus`, `endpoint` etc. For data streams that otherwise fit, but that do not have dataset set we use the value "generic" for the dataset value. `event.dataset` should have the same value as `data_stream.dataset`. Beyond the Elasticsearch data stream naming criteria noted above, the `dataset` value has additional restrictions:   \* Must not contain `-`   \* No longer than 100 characters | constant_keyword |
| data_stream.namespace | A user defined namespace. Namespaces are useful to allow grouping of data. Many users already organize their indices this way, and the data stream naming scheme now provides this best practice as a default. Many users will populate this field with `default`. If no value is used, it falls back to `default`. Beyond the Elasticsearch index naming criteria noted above, `namespace` value has the additional restrictions:   \* Must not contain `-`   \* No longer than 100 characters | constant_keyword |
| data_stream.type | An overarching type for the data stream. Currently allowed values are "logs" and "metrics". We expect to also add "traces" and "synthetics" in the near future. | constant_keyword |
| event.action | The action captured by the event. This describes the information in the event. It is more specific than `event.category`. Examples are `group-add`, `process-started`, `file-created`. The value is normally defined by the implementer. | keyword |
| event.category | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the second level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.category` represents the "big buckets" of ECS categories. For example, filtering on `event.category:process` yields all events relating to process activity. This field is closely related to `event.type`, which is used as a subcategory. This field is an array. This will allow proper categorization of some events that fall in multiple categories. | keyword |
| event.dataset | Name of the dataset. If an event source publishes more than one type of log or events (e.g. access log, error log), the dataset is used to specify which one the event comes from. It's recommended but not required to start the dataset name with the module name, followed by a dot, then the dataset name. | constant_keyword |
| event.id | Unique ID to describe the event. | keyword |
| event.kind | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the highest level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.kind` gives high-level information about what type of information the event contains, without being specific to the contents of the event. For example, values of this field distinguish alert events from metric events. The value of this field can be used to inform how these kinds of events should be handled. They may warrant different retention, different access control, it may also help understand whether the data is coming in at a regular interval or not. | keyword |
| event.module | Name of the module this data is coming from. If your monitoring agent supports the concept of modules or plugins to process events of a given source (e.g. Apache logs), `event.module` should contain the name of this module. | constant_keyword |
| event.outcome | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the lowest level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.outcome` simply denotes whether the event represents a success or a failure from the perspective of the entity that produced the event. Note that when a single transaction is described in multiple events, each event may populate different values of `event.outcome`, according to their perspective. Also note that in the case of a compound event (a single event that contains multiple logical events), this field should be populated with the value that best captures the overall success or failure from the perspective of the event producer. Further note that not all events will have an associated outcome. For example, this field is generally not populated for metric events, events with `event.type:info`, or any events for which an outcome does not make logical sense. | keyword |
| event.type | This is one of four ECS Categorization Fields, and indicates the third level in the ECS category hierarchy. `event.type` represents a categorization "sub-bucket" that, when used along with the `event.category` field values, enables filtering events down to a level appropriate for single visualization. This field is an array. This will allow proper categorization of some events that fall in multiple event types. | keyword |
| http.response.status_code | HTTP response status code. | long |
| input.type | Type of filebeat input. | keyword |
| log.offset | Log offset. | long |
| orchestrator.type | Orchestrator cluster type (e.g. kubernetes, nomad or cloudfoundry). | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.audit.level | Graylog severity level (6 = informational). | long |
| ovh.kubernetes.audit.log_id | Unique Graylog message ID for this audit log entry. | keyword |
| ovh.kubernetes.audit.message | Raw audit log line as stored in OVH Logs Data Platform. | keyword |
| url.original | Unmodified original url as seen in the event source. Note that in network monitoring, the observed URL may be a full URL, whereas in access logs, the URL is often just represented as a path. This field is meant to represent the URL as it was observed, complete or not. | wildcard |
| url.original.text | Multi-field of `url.original`. | match_only_text |
